title: GH-200: GitHub Actions Certification
description: A collection of 80 questions for preparing for the Microsoft GH-200 — GitHub Actions certification.

questions.text: How should you print a debug message in your workflow?

options.text: echo "::debug::Set variable myVariable to true"
options.rationale: The ::debug:: workflow command prints the message only when debug logging is enabled, which is the documented way to emit debug output.

options.text: echo "Set variable MyVariable to true" >> $DEBUG_MESSAGE
options.rationale: Redirecting to $DEBUG_MESSAGE writes to a file path that is not defined on the runner, so no debug message appears.

options.text: echo "::add-mask::Set variable myVariable to true"
options.rationale: The ::add-mask:: command registers a value to be redacted from logs, so it hides secrets instead of printing a debug message.

options.text: echo "debug_message=Set variable myVariable to true" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT
options.rationale: Appending to $GITHUB_OUTPUT sets a step output for later steps and does not produce a debug log entry.

questions.explanation: GitHub Actions provides the ::debug:: command for printing debug messages that only appear when debug mode is enabled. Option C uses ::add-mask:: to mask sensitive info, and D redirects to GITHUB_OUTPUT which is for output variables.

questions.text: As a developer, you are designing a workflow and need to communicate with the runner machine to set environment variables, output values used by other actions, add debug messages to the output logs, and other tasks. Which of the following options should you use?

options.text: composite run step
options.rationale: A composite run step groups shell steps inside an action definition and is not a channel for sending commands to the runner.

options.text: enable debug logging
options.rationale: Enabling debug logging only increases log verbosity and does not set variables, write outputs, or emit debug messages by itself.

options.text: self-hosted runners
options.rationale: Self-hosted runners change where jobs execute, not how a workflow communicates commands and values to the runner.

options.text: environment variables
options.rationale: Environment variables pass values into steps but cannot set other variables, write step outputs, or emit debug messages.

options.text: workflow commands
options.rationale: Workflow commands let a step communicate with the runner to set environment variables, write outputs, and add debug messages.

questions.explanation: Enabling debug logging combined with workflow commands in the steps' run key allows you to communicate with the runner to set environment variables, output values, and add debug messages.

questions.text: When should you use the GITHUB_TOKEN in a workflow?

options.text: when you want to make authenticated calls to the GitHub API
options.rationale: GITHUB_TOKEN is scoped to the repository and authenticates GitHub API calls during the run, which matches the stated need.

options.text: when you want to connect to the runner via SSH
options.rationale: Connecting to the runner over SSH uses runner credentials or keys and has no relationship to GITHUB_TOKEN.

options.text: when you want to access repository-level secrets
options.rationale: Repository secrets are consumed through the secrets context, and GITHUB_TOKEN cannot read or manage the secrets store.

options.text: when you want to call an action from the marketplace
options.rationale: Marketplace actions are referenced by repository path or name and require no GITHUB_TOKEN in order to be called.

questions.explanation: GITHUB_TOKEN is an automatically generated token provided by GitHub for each workflow run, allowing your workflow to authenticate securely to GitHub's API without storing personal access tokens.

questions.text: In which of the following scenarios should you use self-hosted runners? (Each correct answer presents a complete solution. Choose two.)

options.text: when the workflow jobs must be run on Windows 10
options.rationale: GitHub-hosted Windows runners already supply Windows machine images, so the operating system alone does not make self-hosting necessary.

options.text: when jobs must run for longer than 6 hours
options.rationale: GitHub-hosted jobs are cancelled after six hours, so jobs that must run longer require a self-hosted runner.

options.text: when a workflow job needs to install software from the local network
options.rationale: Self-hosted runners sit inside the corporate network, letting jobs install software hosted on internal servers.

options.text: when GitHub Actions minutes must be used for the workflow runs
options.rationale: Included GitHub Actions minutes apply to GitHub-hosted runners, and self-hosted runners do not consume them, so this is not a reason.

options.text: when you want to use macOS runners
options.rationale: macOS runners are available as GitHub-hosted images, so macOS alone does not require a self-hosted runner.

questions.explanation: GitHub-hosted runners have a 6-hour job limit. Self-hosted runners are also required when workflows need access to internal network resources (e.g., licensed software on a company server).

questions.text: As a developer, you need to leverage Redis in your workflow. What is the best way to use Redis on a self-hosted Linux runner without affecting future workflow runs?

options.text: Install Redis on the hosted runner image and place it in a runner group. Specify label: in your job to target the runner group.
options.rationale: GitHub-hosted runner images cannot be modified permanently, and runner groups select runners rather than install software.

options.text: Set up Redis on a separate machine and reference that instance from your job.
options.rationale: A separate Redis machine keeps the service outside the runner, so jobs use it without polluting the runner for future runs.

options.text: Specify container: and services: in your job definition to leverage a Redis service container.
options.rationale: Service containers run alongside one job and disappear with it, and they require Docker on the self-hosted runner for every run.

options.text: Add a run step to your workflow, which dynamically installs and configures Redis as part of your job.
options.rationale: Installing Redis inside a run step modifies the runner host and leaves state that can break later workflow runs.

questions.explanation: Setting up Redis on a separate machine decouples the Redis instance from the self-hosted runner, avoiding environment pollution and conflicts with future workflow runs.

questions.text: You installed specific software on a Linux self-hosted runner. You have users with workflows that need to be able to select the runner based on the identified custom software. Which steps should you perform to prepare the runner and your users to run these workflows? (Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Choose two.)

options.text: Configure the webhook and network to enable GitHub to trigger workflow.
options.rationale: Webhook and network configuration is needed for GitHub connectivity, not for selecting a runner by its installed software.

options.text: Create the group custom-software-on-linux and move the runner into the group.
options.rationale: Runner groups organise access and permissions and do not let users target a runner by the custom software it carries.

options.text: Inform users to identify the runner with the labels custom-software and linux.
options.rationale: Users must know the exact labels for runs-on, so telling them to use custom-software and linux is required.

options.text: Add the label linux to the runner.
options.rationale: The linux label is applied automatically to Linux runners, so adding it manually does not identify the custom software.

options.text: Inform users to identify the runner based on the group.
options.rationale: Groups are used for access control rather than job matching, so users cannot select the runner by group alone.

options.text: Add the label custom-software to the runner.
options.rationale: Adding the custom-software label records the installed software on the runner so that jobs can target it.

questions.explanation: Add the label 'custom-software' to the runner (F), and inform users to target the runner using runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, custom-software] (C).

questions.text: You need to trigger a workflow using the GitHub API for activity that happens outside of GitHub. Which workflow event do you use?

options.text: workflow_run
options.rationale: workflow_run triggers a workflow when another workflow completes, not when activity happens outside GitHub through the REST API.

options.text: deployment
options.rationale: The deployment event fires for deployment activity tracked by GitHub and is not the documented external trigger.

options.text: check_suite
options.rationale: check_suite responds to check suite activity inside GitHub rather than to custom events sent from other systems.

options.text: repository_dispatch
options.rationale: repository_dispatch accepts a REST API call from outside GitHub and starts the workflow with a custom payload.

questions.explanation: repository_dispatch is specifically designed to trigger workflows from outside GitHub using the REST API with a custom event payload.

questions.text: In which locations can actions be referenced by workflows? (Each correct answer presents a complete solution. Choose three.)

options.text: an .action extension file in the repository
options.rationale: An .action extension file is not a supported reference format, since actions are defined by action.yml or action.yaml.

options.text: a published Docker container image on Docker Hub
options.rationale: A Docker container image on Docker Hub can be referenced with the docker:// syntax in a uses key.

options.text: a public NPM registry
options.rationale: The public NPM registry distributes JavaScript packages and is not a location where workflow actions are referenced.

options.text: the runs-on: keyword of a workflow file
options.rationale: The runs-on keyword selects the runner for a job and never references an action to execute.

options.text: the repository's Secrets settings page
options.rationale: The Secrets settings page stores encrypted values and cannot be referenced as the location of an action.

options.text: a separate public repository
options.rationale: A separate public repository can be referenced as owner/repo@ref in the uses key of a step.

options.text: the same repository as the workflow
options.rationale: Actions stored in the same repository are referenced with a relative path such as ./path/to/action.

questions.explanation: Actions can be referenced from: a Docker container image on Docker Hub, a separate public repository (owner/repo@ref), or the same repository as the workflow (relative path).

questions.text: Scheduled workflows run on the:

options.text: specified commit and branch from the workflow YAML file.
options.rationale: The schedule trigger does not read a commit or branch from the workflow YAML and instead uses the default branch head.

options.text: latest commit from the branch named schedule.
options.rationale: There is no branch named schedule by convention, and scheduled runs target the default branch of the repository.

options.text: latest commit and branch on which the workflow was triggered.
options.rationale: The branch that triggered a run is irrelevant for schedules, which always execute against the default branch.

options.text: latest commit from the branch named main.
options.rationale: Only the branch named main would apply if it happened to be the default branch, and the rule is not main specifically.

options.text: latest commit on the default or base branch.
options.rationale: Scheduled workflows run against the latest commit on the default or base branch, which is the documented behaviour.

questions.explanation: Scheduled workflows execute against the latest commit of the branch on which the workflow is defined, always picking the latest state of that branch.

questions.text: Custom environment variables can be defined at multiple levels within a workflow file including: (Each answer presents a complete solution. Choose three.)

options.text: top level.
options.rationale: Top-level env applies to all jobs and steps in the workflow, so it is a valid definition level.

options.text: step level.
options.rationale: Step-level env applies only to that single step, which is one of the supported definition levels for custom variables.

options.text: default level.
options.rationale: There is no default level for custom environment variables in a GitHub Actions workflow file.

options.text: runner level.
options.rationale: Runner-level configuration is not part of the workflow env hierarchy and cannot define custom variables.

options.text: job level.
options.rationale: Job-level env applies to every step in that job, which is a valid definition level.

options.text: stage level.
options.rationale: Stages are an Azure DevOps concept, and GitHub Actions workflows have no stage level for variables.

questions.explanation: Environment variables can be defined at: top level (available to all jobs), job level (available to all steps in the job), and step level (available only during that step).

questions.text: You are a DevOps engineer working on deployment workflows. You need to execute the deploy job only if the current branch name is feature-branch. Which code snippet will help you implement the conditional execution of the job?

options.text: if: github.ref_name == 'feature-branch'
options.rationale: github.ref_name returns the short branch name, so comparing it with feature-branch implements the required condition.

options.text: if: github.branch.name == 'feature-branch'
options.rationale: github.branch is not a valid context object, so this expression cannot be evaluated by the workflow.

options.text: if: github.ref.name == 'feature-branch'
options.rationale: github.ref.name is not a valid property path because github.ref is a string with no nested name field.

options.text: if: github.branch_name == 'feature-branch'
options.rationale: github.branch_name is not a defined context property, and GitHub Actions only exposes the documented github context fields.

questions.explanation: github.ref holds the full ref (refs/heads/feature-branch) and github.ref.name extracts just the branch name. github.ref_name is not a valid property path — it's accessed as github.ref.name.

questions.text: What are the mandatory requirements for publishing GitHub Actions to the GitHub Marketplace? (Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Choose two.)

options.text: The action can be either in a public or private repository.
options.rationale: Marketplace actions must be published from public repositories, so a private repository is not permitted.

options.text: The action's metadata file must be in the root directory of the repository.
options.rationale: The action metadata file, action.yml or action.yaml, must sit in the root directory of the repository.

options.text: The action's name cannot match a user or organization on GitHub unless the user or organization owner is publishing the action.
options.rationale: The action name must not impersonate an existing user or organization unless that owner publishes the action.

options.text: The name should match with one of the existing GitHub Marketplace categories.
options.rationale: The action name does not have to match an existing Marketplace category, since categories are chosen separately.

options.text: Each repository can contain a collection of actions as long as they are under the same Marketplace category.
options.rationale: A repository can contain only one published Marketplace action, so a collection of actions is not allowed.

questions.explanation: The action.yml/action.yaml file must be in the root directory (B). The action name cannot impersonate an existing GitHub user or organization unless the owner is publishing it (C). Marketplace actions must be in public repositories.

questions.text: Which of the following is the proper syntax to specify a custom environment variable named MY_VARIABLE with the value my-value?

options.text:
var:
  MY_VARIABLE = my-value
options.rationale: var is not a GitHub Actions keyword, and the equals sign does not create valid YAML mapping syntax.

options.text:
environment:
  MY_VARIABLE = my-value
options.rationale: environment is not used to define variables in this form, and the equals sign is invalid YAML mapping syntax.

options.text:
var:
  MY_VARIABLE: my-value
options.rationale: var is not a recognised workflow keyword for defining environment variables anywhere in the file.

options.text:
env:
  MY_VARIABLE = my-value
options.rationale: The env keyword is correct, but an equals sign does not create a YAML key-value mapping.

options.text:
environment:
  MY_VARIABLE: my-value
options.rationale: environment references a deployment environment and does not define a variable mapping in this form.

options.text:
env:
  MY_VARIABLE: my-value
options.rationale: The env keyword takes a YAML mapping, so env followed by a colon-separated key and value is the valid syntax.

questions.explanation: GitHub Actions uses the 'env' keyword to define environment variables. Options using 'var' or 'environment' are invalid keywords.

questions.text: As a DevOps engineer, you need to define a deployment workflow that runs after the build workflow has successfully completed. Without modifying the build workflow, which trigger should you define in the deployment workflow?

options.text: repository_dispatch
options.rationale: repository_dispatch requires an external API call and would need changes to how the build workflow is started.

options.text: workflow_dispatch
options.rationale: workflow_dispatch requires a manual request and does not chain automatically after the build workflow finishes.

options.text: workflow_exec
options.rationale: workflow_exec is not a GitHub Actions event and does not exist in the workflow syntax.

options.text: workflow_run
options.rationale: workflow_run triggers on completion of another workflow and can be filtered so it runs only for successful conclusions.

questions.explanation: workflow_run lets you trigger one workflow after another has finished, without needing to modify the original workflow. It can be configured to run only if the triggering workflow completed successfully.

questions.text: Which step is using the dbserver environment variable correctly?

options.text:
- name: Hello world
  run: echo $dbserver
  variables:
    dbserver: orgserver1
options.rationale: variables is not a valid step keyword, so the value is never exposed to the run command.

options.text:
- name: Hello world
  run: echo $dbserver
  env:
  - name: dbserver
    value: orgserver1
options.rationale: env must be a mapping rather than a list of name and value entries, so this step syntax is invalid.

options.text:
- name: Hello world
  run: echo $dbserver
  environment:
    dbserver: orgserver1
options.rationale: environment refers to a deployment environment and does not define variables available to the step.

options.text:
- name: Hello world
  run: echo $dbserver
  env:
    dbserver: orgserver1
options.rationale: A step-level env mapping with a key-value pair exposes dbserver to the run command correctly.

questions.explanation: The correct syntax uses the 'env' key at the step level with a key-value pair. Options A, B, and C use incorrect keywords ('variables', list syntax, 'environment') that are not valid in this context.

questions.text: In which scenarios could the GITHUB_TOKEN be used? (Each correct answer presents a complete solution. Choose two.)

options.text: to create a repository secret
options.rationale: Creating repository secrets requires repository administration permission, which the automatically generated GITHUB_TOKEN is never granted.

options.text: to add a member to an organization
options.rationale: Adding organization members requires organization-level administration permissions that the repository-scoped GITHUB_TOKEN never receives or holds.

options.text: to read from the file system on the runner
options.rationale: The runner file system is accessed directly by shell commands in steps, not by the GITHUB_TOKEN credential.

options.text: to publish to GitHub Packages
options.rationale: GITHUB_TOKEN can be granted packages write permission, which allows the workflow to publish to GitHub Packages.

options.text: to create issues in the repo
options.rationale: GITHUB_TOKEN can hold issues write permission, allowing the workflow to create issues in the repository.

options.text: to leverage a self-hosted runner
options.rationale: Selecting a self-hosted runner is a runs-on configuration and has nothing to do with GITHUB_TOKEN.

questions.explanation: GITHUB_TOKEN has write permissions to the packages scope (D) and the issues scope (E). It cannot create repository secrets or add organization members, as those require higher-level tokens.

questions.text: As a developer, which of the following snippets will enable you to run the commands npm ci and npm run build as part of a workflow?

options.text:
- run: |
    npm ci
    npm run build
options.rationale: The run keyword with the pipe operator executes both commands as separate lines in the job default shell.

options.text:
- shell:
    npm ci
    npm run build
options.rationale: shell expects a shell name rather than commands, so the npm commands are never executed.

options.text:
- run: |
    npm ci
    npm run build
  shell: nodejs
options.rationale: nodejs is not a supported shell value, and valid values include bash, sh, pwsh, python, cmd and powershell.

options.text:
- run:
    npm ci
    npm run build
options.rationale: A run key without a value or block scalar leaves the commands unparsed and makes the step invalid.

options.text:
- shell: |
    npm ci
    npm run build
options.rationale: shell cannot take a block of commands and must name an available shell executable instead.

questions.explanation: Option C uses the 'run' keyword with the '|' multi-line operator to run both commands as separate lines, and specifies 'shell: nodejs' to execute in the Node.js environment.

questions.text: What is the smallest scope for an environment variable?

options.text: the workflow settings
options.rationale: Workflow settings is not a variable scope, and the workflow env mapping is broader than job or step scope.

options.text: the workflow env mapping
options.rationale: The workflow env mapping applies to all jobs and steps, making it the broadest scope rather than the smallest.

options.text: a job
options.rationale: A job scope covers every step in that job, so it is wider than the scope of a single step.

options.text: a step
options.rationale: Step-level env applies to one step only and overrides wider scopes, making it the smallest scope.

questions.explanation: According to this question, the smallest scope for a custom environment variable in a workflow file is the job level. Step-level env variables are scoped to a single step, but the question refers to the smallest named scope in the workflow structure.

questions.text: Which workflow event is used to manually trigger a workflow run?

options.text: status
options.rationale: The status event reacts to commit status updates and cannot start a workflow on manual request.

options.text: workflow_dispatch
options.rationale: workflow_dispatch defines a workflow that can be started manually from the UI, API or command line.

options.text: workflow_run
options.rationale: workflow_run starts a workflow after another workflow completes, rather than in response to a manual trigger from a user.

options.text: create
options.rationale: The create event fires when a branch or tag is created and does not respond to manual requests.

questions.explanation: workflow_run triggers a workflow when another workflow is completed. Note: workflow_dispatch is also used for manual triggers via UI/API.

questions.text: Where should workflow files be stored to be triggered by events in a repository?

options.text: anywhere
options.rationale: Workflow files are not discovered from arbitrary locations, since GitHub only scans the required .github/workflows directory.

options.text: Nowhere; they must be attached to an action in the GitHub user interface.
options.rationale: Workflows are YAML files stored in the repository and are not attached through the GitHub user interface.

options.text: .github/workflows/
options.rationale: .github/workflows/ is the required directory, and GitHub only discovers workflow files stored in that path.

options.text: .workflows/
options.rationale: .workflows/ lacks the .github prefix, so GitHub does not detect workflows placed in that directory.

options.text: .github/actions/
options.rationale: .github/actions/ stores action definitions and is not the directory where workflow files must be placed for GitHub to find them.

questions.explanation: Per the exam answer key: .workflows/. Note: The actual GitHub documentation specifies .github/workflows/ as the correct location.

questions.text: Your organization is managing secrets using GitHub encrypted secrets, including a secret named SuperSecret. As a developer, you need to create a version of that secret that contains a different value for use in a workflow scoped to a specific repository named MyRepo. How should you store the secret to access your specific version within your workflow?

options.text: Create MyRepo_SuperSecret in GitHub encrypted secrets to specify the scope to MyRepo.
options.rationale: A name prefixed with the repository name is just an ordinary secret called MyRepo_SuperSecret; GitHub resolves secrets by exact name and has no prefix-based scoping.

options.text: Create a duplicate entry for SuperSecret in the encrypted secret store and specify MyRepo as the scope.
options.rationale: An organization secret holds one value for every repository it is shared with, so a duplicate entry scoped to MyRepo cannot carry a different value.

options.text: Create a file with the SuperSecret information in the .github/secrets folder in MyRepo.
options.rationale: GitHub Actions never reads secret values from files in the repository, and a .github/secrets folder is not a supported secrets store.

options.text: Create and access SuperSecret from the secrets store in MyRepo.
options.rationale: A repository secret named SuperSecret in MyRepo overrides the organization secret of the same name, giving that repository its own value.

questions.explanation: GitHub Actions prioritizes repository secrets over organization secrets when the repository secret name incorporates the repository name as a prefix (e.g., MyRepo_SuperSecret overrides the org-level SuperSecret).

questions.text: Which default GitHub environment variable indicates the owner and repository name?

options.text: GITHUB_REPOSITORY
options.rationale: GITHUB_REPOSITORY holds the owner and repository name together, such as octocat/hello-world, so it supplies both values in one variable.

options.text: GITHUB_WORKFLOW_REPO
options.rationale: GITHUB_WORKFLOW_REPO is not a default GitHub Actions variable, so a workflow referencing it receives an empty value.

options.text: ENV_REPOSITORY
options.rationale: ENV_REPOSITORY is not defined by GitHub Actions, because automatic variables use the GITHUB_ prefix instead of ENV_.

options.text: REPOSITORY_NAME
options.rationale: REPOSITORY_NAME is not a default environment variable, and the owner plus repository value comes only from GITHUB_REPOSITORY.

questions.explanation: GITHUB_REPOSITORY contains the owner and repository name in the format 'owner/repository' (e.g., 'myuser/myrepo').

questions.text: You are a DevOps engineer in ABC Corp. You need to schedule your deployment workflow twice a week at 7:45 UTC every Wednesday and Saturday. What is the appropriate YAML structure?

options.rationale: The cron expression is correct, but it sits directly under on instead of under the required schedule key, so the trigger is invalid.

options.text:
on:
  cron:
  - schedule: '45 7 * * 3,6'
options.rationale: The list item nests schedule inside cron, which reverses the required structure of a schedule event containing cron entries.

options.text:
on:
  schedule:
  - cron: '45 7 * * 3,6'
options.rationale: The schedule event takes a list of cron entries, and this block defines one entry at 07:45 UTC on Wednesday and Saturday.

options.text:
on:
  schedule: '45 7 * * 3,6'
options.rationale: The schedule event expects a list of mappings with cron keys, not a bare string, so this syntax is rejected.

questions.explanation: The schedule trigger must use the 'schedule' keyword under 'on:', and each cron entry must be defined as a list item with '- cron'. The cron expression '45 7 * * 3,6' means 7:45 UTC on Wednesday (3) and Saturday (6).

questions.text: You need to create new workflows to deploy to an unfamiliar cloud provider. What is the fastest and safest way to begin?

options.text: Create a custom action to wrap the cloud provider's CLI.
options.rationale: Writing a custom action around the provider CLI means designing and maintaining scripts before any deployment, which is slower and riskier than reusing published actions.

options.text: Search GitHub Marketplace for verified actions published by the cloud provider.
options.rationale: Marketplace actions published by the cloud provider are verified and maintained by that vendor, giving a supported integration without custom code.

options.text: Use the actions/jenkins-plugin action to utilize an existing Jenkins plugin for the cloud provider.
options.rationale: There is no actions/jenkins-plugin action, and a Jenkins plugin for the provider would not run inside a GitHub Actions job.

options.text: Search GitHub Marketplace for actions created by GitHub.
options.rationale: Actions created by GitHub cover GitHub tooling rather than the unfamiliar provider's services, so they do not implement that deployment.

options.text: Download the CLI for the cloud provider and review the associated documentation.
options.rationale: Reading the provider CLI documentation is useful research but still requires building the deployment automation yourself, which is not the fastest path.

questions.explanation: Verified actions from the GitHub Marketplace published by the cloud provider are maintained by the provider, security-reviewed by GitHub, and allow quick integration without writing custom scripts.

questions.text: Which of the following scenarios requires a developer to explicitly use the GITHUB_TOKEN or github.token secret within a workflow? (Choose two.)

options.text: passing the GITHUB_TOKEN secret to an action that requires a token as an input
options.rationale: An action that takes a token as an input receives nothing automatically, so the workflow must pass the token expression explicitly.

options.text: making an authenticated GitHub API request
options.rationale: Direct API calls made with curl or another client need an explicit token expression in the request header to authenticate.

options.text: checking out source code with the actions/checkout@v3 action
options.rationale: actions/checkout reads the token from its own default configuration, so workflows do not pass the token explicitly.

options.text: assigning non-default permissions to the GITHUB_TOKEN
options.rationale: Changing token permissions uses the permissions key, which adjusts the token without explicitly passing its value anywhere.

questions.explanation: Explicitly passing GITHUB_TOKEN is needed when an action requires it as an input (A) and when making direct authenticated API requests via curl or API clients (B). actions/checkout@v3 uses it implicitly, and permissions assignment doesn't require passing the token explicitly.

questions.text: By default, which workflows can use an action stored in internal repository? (Each answer presents a complete solution. Choose two.)

options.text: selected public repositories outside of the enterprise
options.rationale: Actions stored in internal repositories are not exposed to public repositories outside the enterprise, so those workflows cannot use them.

options.text: internal repositories owned by the same organization as the enterprise
options.rationale: Internal repositories in the same organization can use actions from internal repositories, which is the default visibility within the enterprise.

options.text: public repositories owned by the same organization as the enterprise
options.rationale: Actions from internal repositories are shared with internal and private repositories in the enterprise by default, not with public repositories.

options.text: private repositories owned by an organization of the enterprise
options.rationale: Private repositories owned by any organization in the same enterprise can use internal repository actions under the default policy.

questions.explanation: Actions stored in internal repositories can be used by: internal repositories in the same organization (B), and private repositories in any organization within the same enterprise (D).

questions.text: Which default environment variable specifies the branch or tag that triggered a workflow?

options.text: GITHUB_REF
options.rationale: GITHUB_REF contains the fully formed ref that triggered the run, such as refs/heads/main for a branch or refs/tags/v1 for a tag.

options.text: GITHUB_BRANCH
options.rationale: GITHUB_BRANCH is not a default GitHub Actions variable, so a workflow that references it receives an empty value.

options.text: ENV_BRANCH
options.rationale: ENV_BRANCH is not defined by GitHub Actions, because automatic variables use the GITHUB_ prefix rather than ENV_.

options.text: GITHUB_TAG
options.rationale: GITHUB_TAG is not a default variable at all; tag information is carried in GITHUB_REF and GITHUB_REF_NAME.

questions.explanation: Per the exam answer key: GITHUB_BRANCH. Note: The actual GitHub documentation uses GITHUB_REF as the variable containing the branch/tag ref.

questions.text: As a developer, you need to add the correct syntax to allow a workflow file to be triggered by multiple types of events. Which two code blocks should you add starting at line 5? (Each correct answer presents a complete solution. Choose two.)

options.text: on: [push, pull_request]
options.rationale: The array form of on lists push and pull_request together, which triggers the workflow for both events.

options.text:
on:
  branches:

questions.text: You are reaching your organization's storage limit for GitHub artifacts and packages. What should you do to prevent the storage limit from being reached? (Each correct answer presents a complete solution. Choose two.)

options.text: Use self-hosted runners for all workflow runs.
options.rationale: Self-hosted runners change where jobs execute, but artifacts and logs still upload to and consume GitHub storage.

options.text: Delete artifacts from the repositories manually.
options.rationale: Deleting stored artifacts removes them immediately, which lowers current usage below the organization storage limit.

options.text: Configure the artifact and log retention period.
options.rationale: A shorter retention period deletes artifacts and logs automatically, preventing storage from growing to the limit.

options.text: Disable branch protections in the repository.
options.rationale: Branch protection settings do not affect stored artifacts or logs, so disabling them frees no storage.

options.text: Configure the repo to use Git Large File Storage.
options.rationale: Git LFS stores large files inside Git, and enabling it adds storage usage rather than reducing artifact storage.

questions.explanation: Manually deleting artifacts (B) frees space immediately. Configuring a retention period (C) automates cleanup by deleting artifacts and logs after a set time. Self-hosted runners don't affect GitHub's artifact storage.

options.text: 60 days

options.text: 14 days
options.rationale: Fourteen days is shorter than the documented limit, and GitHub does not fail waiting runs at that point.

options.text: 7 days
options.rationale: Seven days is not a GitHub Actions limit, and waiting deployments are not failed after one week.

questions.explanation: GitHub Actions workflows waiting for approval can remain in the 'Waiting' state for up to 60 days before automatically failing, preventing indefinitely stalled workflows.

questions.text: How can a workflow deploy mitigate the risk of multiple workflow runs that are deploying to a single cloud environment simultaneously? (Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Choose two.)

options.text: Reference the mutex in the task performing the deployment.
options.rationale: GitHub Actions has no mutex object, so a task cannot reference one to serialize deployments.

options.text: Set the concurrency in the deployment job to 1.
options.rationale: The concurrency key takes a group name rather than a number, so setting it to 1 is invalid syntax.

options.text: Specify a target environment in the deployment job.
options.rationale: A shared target environment routes every deployment through the same environment and its protection rules, coordinating releases to it.

options.text: Specify a concurrency scope in the workflow.
options.rationale: A workflow concurrency group with a shared name allows only one run in that group to proceed at a time.

options.text: Configure the mutex setting in the environment.
options.rationale: Environments have no mutex setting; their protection rules cover reviewers, wait timers, and branch policies instead.

options.text: Pass the mutex into the deployment job.
options.rationale: A mutex cannot be passed into a job because GitHub Actions has no mutex feature or value to pass.

questions.explanation: Specifying a target environment (C) enables protection rules like single active deployment behavior. Specifying a concurrency scope (D) with the 'concurrency' keyword ensures only one job with the same group runs at a time.

questions.text: Disabling a workflow allows you to stop a workflow from being triggered without deleting the file. In which scenarios would temporarily disabling a workflow be most useful? (Each correct answer presents a complete solution. Choose two.)

options.text: A runner needs to have diagnostic logging enabled.
options.rationale: Enabling diagnostic logging on a runner is a runner configuration task; it does not require stopping workflow triggers, so disabling the workflow is irrelevant here.

options.text: A workflow error produces too many, or wrong, requests, impacting external services negatively.
options.rationale: Correct. A buggy workflow sending too many or wrong requests harms external services, so disabling it immediately stops the damage while the file is fixed.

options.text: A workflow is configured to run on self-hosted runners.
options.rationale: Running on self-hosted runners is an infrastructure choice, not a failure condition, and disabling the workflow does not change or improve runner configuration.

options.text: A workflow sends requests to a service that is down.
options.rationale: Correct. When a dependent service is down, disabling the workflow stops repeated failing runs and conserves resources until the service recovers.

options.text: A workflow needs to be changed from running on a schedule to a manual trigger.
options.rationale: Changing from a scheduled to a manual trigger is done by editing the trigger in the workflow file, not by temporarily disabling the workflow.

questions.explanation: Disabling is most useful when a buggy workflow overloads external services (B), or when a dependency is down and the workflow keeps failing unnecessarily (D). This conserves resources and prevents further damage.

questions.text: What are the two ways to pass data between jobs? (Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Choose two.)

options.rationale: Data storage is a vague term and is not a GitHub Actions mechanism for passing values between jobs.

options.text: Use the copy action with cache parameter to cache the data.
options.rationale: There is no copy action with a cache parameter for passing data between jobs; caching is meant for dependencies.

options.text: Use the copy action with restore parameter to restore the data from the cache.
options.rationale: A copy action with a restore parameter does not exist; cache restoration is performed by actions/cache, not a copy action.

options.text: Use artifact storage.
options.rationale: Correct. Artifact storage uploads files in one job and downloads them in another, handling large outputs.

options.text: Use job outputs.
options.rationale: Correct. Job outputs pass small string values to dependent jobs through needs expressions in the workflow.

options.text: Use the copy action to save the data that should be passed in the artifacts folder.
options.rationale: No copy action writes data into an artifacts folder for job-to-job transfer; artifacts use upload and download actions.

questions.explanation: Artifact storage (D) allows passing large files between jobs. Job outputs (E) allow passing small string values directly between jobs using expressions.

questions.text: As a developer, you are optimizing a GitHub workflow that uses and produces many different files. You need to determine when to use caching versus workflow artifacts. Which two statements are true? (Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Choose two.)

options.text: Use artifacts to access the GitHub Package Registry and download a package for a workflow.
options.rationale: Artifacts are not used to access the GitHub Package Registry; packages are downloaded with package managers or registry actions.

options.text: Use caching when reusing files that change rarely between jobs or workflow runs.
options.rationale: Correct. Caching is intended for dependencies and files that rarely change, speeding up repeated jobs and workflow runs.

options.text: Use caching to store cache entries for up to 30 days between accesses.
options.rationale: Cache entries expire after seven days without access by default, not thirty days, and retention is not the selection criterion.

options.text: Use artifacts when referencing files produced by a job after a workflow has ended.
options.rationale: Correct. Artifacts persist after the workflow finishes so later jobs or people can retrieve the produced files.

questions.explanation: Caching (B) is ideal for rarely-changing dependencies that speed up subsequent runs. Artifacts (D) are for storing workflow outputs that need to be accessed after the workflow finishes.

questions.text: What is the right method to ensure users approve a workflow before the next step proceeds?

options.text: creating a branch protection rule and only allow certain users access
options.rationale: A branch protection rule governs merges into a branch; it cannot pause a running job before its next step or gate a deployment workflow.

options.text: granting users workflow approval permissions
options.rationale: GitHub has no workflow approval permission in its permission model; permissions grant token scopes, not interactive approval of running workflows.

options.text: adding users as required reviewers for an environment
options.rationale: Correct. Environment protection rules support required reviewers, so a job pauses when it requests the environment and resumes only after an approver signs off.

options.text: granting users repository approval permission
options.rationale: There is no repository approval permission; repository roles and Actions permissions do not provide a mechanism to approve a workflow mid-run.

questions.explanation: Granting users workflow approval permissions directly addresses the requirement of user approval before a workflow proceeds to the next step.

options.rationale: pull_request synchronize fires on new commits pushed to the pull request, which is unrelated to the provider's check completion.

options.text: Docker container action

options.text: Bash script action

questions.text: Which workflow commands send information from the runner? (Each correct answer presents a complete solution. Choose two.)

options.rationale: Reading environment variables consumes information already present on the runner; it does not send information out.

options.text: setting a debug message
options.rationale: Correct. The ::debug:: workflow command emits a debug message from the runner into the job log.

options.text: populating variables in a Dockerfile
options.rationale: Populating variables in a Dockerfile is a build-time container concern, not a runner workflow command that sends information.

options.text: setting output parameters
options.rationale: Correct. Writing name=value to the GITHUB_OUTPUT file sets step outputs that later steps can read.

questions.text: You are a DevOps engineer working on a custom action. You want to conditionally run a script at the start of the action, before the main entrypoint. Which code block should be used to define the metadata file for your custom action?

options.rationale: Referencing package.json is common for JavaScript actions but does not itself define the action type; runs.using does.
